title: Donkey Kong
description: Donkey Kong, Nintendo's 1981 breakthrough, introduced Mario as Jumpman, a carpenter rescuing Pauline from a giant ape at the top of a construction site. The player climbs girders, jumps barrels that roll down the scaffolding, and rides elevators and conveyor belts across four distinct stages. It established the platform genre and the character who would become gaming's most famous mascot.
body:
Donkey Kong, Nintendo's 1981 breakthrough, introduced Mario as Jumpman, a carpenter rescuing Pauline from a giant ape at the top of a construction site. The player climbs girders, jumps barrels that roll down the scaffolding, and rides elevators and conveyor belts across four distinct stages. It established the platform genre and the character who would become gaming's most famous mascot.

The tribute demo runs a side-view course 18 steps long with obstacles at positions 5, 9, 14: the player types jump or run each tick, jumping over each obstacle to reach the end with lives to spare. It is an original miniature inspired by the platforming idea, not a copy of the arcade game.

Barrels roll down ladders as well as girders, so the safest climb is a ladder the barrels are not using. The hammer is a brief blessing: grabbing it clears barrels for a few seconds, but it also stops the player from climbing, so it should be used on flat ground, not mid-ladder.
controls: Type jump/run each tick to cross the course, quit to stop.

title: Donkey Kong Jr.
description: Donkey Kong Jr., Nintendo's 1982 sequel, flips the story: Mario has caged Donkey Kong, and his son must climb vines and chains to free him. Junior climbs by gripping two vines at once, slides down chains, and drops fruit onto enemies below. The vine-climbing mechanic made movement feel different from the original's ladders.
body:
Donkey Kong Jr., Nintendo's 1982 sequel, flips the story: Mario has caged Donkey Kong, and his son must climb vines and chains to free him. Junior climbs by gripping two vines at once, slides down chains, and drops fruit onto enemies below. The vine-climbing mechanic made movement feel different from the original's ladders.

title: Jump Bug
description: Jump Bug, Hoei's 1981 platform game, is an early side-scrolling platformer where a car jumps over gaps and enemies across rolling hills and city streets. The game scrolls continuously, and the player must time jumps over pits and obstacles while shooting or avoiding hazards, making it a precursor to the scrolling platformers that followed.
body:
Jump Bug, Hoei's 1981 platform game, is an early side-scrolling platformer where a car jumps over gaps and enemies across rolling hills and city streets. The game scrolls continuously, and the player must time jumps over pits and obstacles while shooting or avoiding hazards, making it a precursor to the scrolling platformers that followed.

Psychic-5, Jaleco's 1987 platform game, stars five children with psychic powers exploring a demon's mansion. Each child has a different ability, from hovering to hammer attacks, and the player switches between them to reach hidden areas and defeat the demon's minions. Its character-switching was unusual for arcade platformers.

The tribute demo runs a side-view course 20 steps long with obstacles at positions 6, 10, 15, 18: the player types jump or run each tick, jumping over each obstacle to reach the end with lives to spare. It is an original miniature inspired by the platforming idea, not a copy of the arcade game.

Switching characters is the puzzle: the hovering child reaches high ledges, while the hammer child breaks barriers, so the route should be planned around who is needed where. Sticking with one child through a whole stage wastes the team's strengths.
